topic: What evidence-based care means at our clinic

slides.headline: What 'evidence-based' means in practice
slides.sub: Research, your practitioner's experience and what matters to you, together.

slides.title: Three parts, not one
slides.body: Evidence-based care blends current research, your practitioner's clinical experience, and your goals and preferences. Research alone doesn't know you play netball on Tuesdays or work ten-hour days.

slides.title: Active care usually comes first
slides.body: For many muscle and joint problems, current guidelines put exercise, education and a gradual return to activity first. Hands-on treatment can help you move more comfortably as part of that plan.

slides.title: Honest when evidence is thin
slides.body: Some treatments have stronger support than others. We'll explain what's known, what's uncertain and why we're suggesting something, so you can make an informed choice about your care.

slides.title: We measure, then adjust
slides.body: Strength tests, range of movement, questionnaires or how far you can walk give us something to track. If progress stalls, we change the plan or refer on rather than repeat the same session.

slides.title: Referring when it fits
slides.body: Sometimes the right next step is your GP, a specialist or another practitioner on our team. With physio, chiro, Pilates and remedial massage under one roof, we can share one plan.

slides.headline: Care you can ask questions about
slides.body: Our team at Hybrid Physiotherapy will explain the reasoning behind your plan and keep it focused on your goals. Book online — link in bio.

caption:
'Evidence-based' gets used a lot. Here's what it looks like in a real appointment.

It's three things working together: current research, your practitioner's clinical experience, and your own goals and preferences. A plan that ignores any one of those usually doesn't stick.

In practice, that means active care like exercise and education usually comes first, with hands-on treatment as a helpful add-on. It means being upfront when the evidence for something is thin. And it means measuring progress, then changing the plan or referring on if things aren't moving.

Questions about why we're suggesting something are always welcome. Book online via the link in bio.

General information only — not a substitute for an individual assessment.

story.body: Research, experience and your goals, together. Ask us why we're suggesting anything. We'll explain.
